Creating Mocks with Jest

jest.fn(), mockResolvedValue, and asserting what a mock was actually called with.

Jest's tool for creating a mock function is jest.fn() — it returns a callable function that does nothing on its own, but remembers every call made to it and can be told what to return. A fake Prisma client, for the methods ticket.service.js actually uses, is just an ordinary object built out of these:

// Figure 2.17: a fake Prisma client (tests/unit/ticket.service.test.js, excerpt)
const mockPrisma = {
  ticket: {
    findMany: jest.fn(),
    findUnique: jest.fn(),
    create: jest.fn(),
  },
};

Every real Prisma method is async, so a test needs its fake version to return a Promise too, resolved to whatever value that test wants to pretend came back from the database — mockResolvedValue does exactly that:

// Figure 2.18: controlling and inspecting a mock (tests/unit/ticket.service.test.js, excerpt)
it('getAllTickets returns whatever Prisma finds', async () => {
  const seeded = [{ id: 1, subject: 'Cannot log in' }];
  mockPrisma.ticket.findMany.mockResolvedValue(seeded);

  const tickets = await getAllTickets();

  expect(tickets).toBe(seeded);
  expect(mockPrisma.ticket.findMany).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
});

mockPrisma.ticket.findMany.mockResolvedValue(seeded) is the control half from the previous slide: whatever calls findMany() next gets back seeded, immediately, with no real query. toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) is the inspection half: an assertion not about a return value at all, but about whether — and how — the mock itself was used. beforeEach(() => jest.clearAllMocks()) resets every mock's call history and configured return value between tests, so one test's mockResolvedValue never leaks into the next.
